title: GRU
matchup: Cho et al. (2014) vs Gers, Schmidhuber & Cummins (2000)
question: Do the GRU's relationship to LSTM and its citations support Schmidhuber's claim that the forget-gate work deserved explicit credit?

usual_credit.summary: Kyunghyun Cho and colleagues in Yoshua Bengio's group introduced the gated recurrent unit (GRU) in 2014 in a paper on encoder-decoder models for machine translation, as a simpler recurrent unit with a reset gate and an update gate. Chung et al. (2014) compared GRU and LSTM units empirically, and the GRU became a common alternative to the LSTM.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber says the GRU is a variant of the vanilla LSTM architecture with forget gates, which Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins introduced in 2000, and that the GRU papers cited only the 1997 LSTM paper, which did not yet have forget gates, while giving the variant a new name. He adds that under the finite-precision assumptions of the Weiss, Goldberg and Yahav study, GRUs lack the unbounded counting behavior available to LSTMs, and that Google Brain found them to work less well for challenging translation tasks.

response.summary: Cho and colleagues describe their unit as motivated by LSTM but simpler to compute and implement, and Chung and colleagues compare the two units empirically rather than claiming to have invented gated recurrence. Their citations include the 1997 LSTM paper and Graves's account, but not the forget-gate paper. Independent studies by Britz and colleagues and by Weiss, Goldberg and Yahav examine translation quality and counting under specified conditions, which should not be read as a universal ranking on every task. The papers acknowledge an LSTM relationship, but do not directly answer Schmidhuber's complaint about the missing forget-gate citation.

agreed_facts: Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins introduced the forget gate for LSTM in 'Learning to Forget: Continual Prediction with LSTM', published in Neural Computation in October 2000 after an earlier version at ICANN 1999.
Cho et al. posted the GRU paper on arXiv on 3 June 2014, and Chung et al. posted their comparison of GRU and LSTM units on 11 December 2014.

Cho et al. describe the GRU as motivated by the LSTM unit, cite Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997), and do not cite Gers et al. (2000); Chung et al. cite the 1997 paper for LSTM and follow the implementation in Graves (2013).
The GRU has a reset gate and an update gate and no separate output gate, while the LSTM unit with a forget gate has input, forget and output gates.
crux: Whether the GRU counts as a new architecture or as a simplification of the forget-gate LSTM whose source should have been cited, and whether citing the 1997 LSTM paper alone was an adequate acknowledgement when the gating idea appears in the 2000 paper. The architectural differences are documented; their significance for invention credit is the question.
